en_simple_draft.text: *Liṅga* in the strict sense is what was just defined; that which differs from it in one or both respects is no true *liṅga* for inferring the *sādhya*. Śrīdhara glosses the *Vaiśeṣika-sūtra* III-i-15 *aprasiddho 'napadeśo 'san sandigdhaś ca*: *anapadeśa* = 'not a *hetu*'; *apadeśa* = *hetu*. *Aprasiddha* includes the *viruddha* (contradictory) and the *asādhāraṇa* (too-narrow) *hetu*s — both lack ascertained concomitance with the *sādhya*. *Asat* covers the *asiddha* *hetu* — known to be concomitant with the *sādhya* but not present in the *pakṣa*. *Sandigdha* is the *anaikāntika* *hetu* — present in the *pakṣa* but doubtfully concomitant with the *sādhya*. Where no ascertainment 'this is invariably concomitant with that' obtains, the property cannot be a true *liṅga* even if it accompanies the *pakṣa* — the *vyāpti-smṛti* is a necessary accessory of inferential cognition.

en_simple_draft.text: Śrīdhara's expanded commentary on *parārtha-anumāna* and the inferential process — one of the longest blocks in this stretch. The mechanics: when one cognisant of the invariable concomitance ('wherever there is smoke there is fire; wherever no fire, no smoke') has a doubt-free perception of smoke and recalls the *vyāpti*, an inferential cognition of fire arises. He answers the Bauddha *tādātmya–tadutpatti* doctrine (Dignāga–Dharmakīrti's view that *vyāpti* rests on either identity-of-essence or causal origination), refusing both as the ground of *vyāpti*; the long *apoha* sub-debate is treated as well. *Kārya-kāraṇa-bhāva*, *svābhāvika-sambandha*, *svarūpa-sambandha*, *sapakṣa-vipakṣa-vṛtti*, and the structure of the trairūpya are all examined. The *upanaya* (minor premise) is dispensable in *svārtha-anumāna* but indispensable in *parārtha-anumāna* because it alone establishes *pakṣa-dharmatā* for the second person. The *pramiti* (cognitive fruit) is either the cognition of fire itself or of fire's desirable/undesirable character. The block closes the analysis of inference for oneself; the five members of *parārtha-anumāna* (*pratijñā*, *hetu/apadeśa*, *udāharaṇa/nidarśana*, *upanaya/anusandhāna*, *nigamana/pratyāmnāya*) are taken up in the texts that follow.

en_simple_draft.text: *Śabda-pramāṇa* and the other supposed independent means of knowledge are included under *anumāna*. Śrīdhara examines the Nyāya–Mīmāṃsā–Bauddha śabda debates at length. Verbal cognition depends on the *vyāpti* between a word and its meaning, and that *vyāpti* is *sāṅketika* — fixed by convention, not by nature: the same word *cora* means 'cooked rice' in the south and 'thief' in Āryāvarta, a usage that refutes any inherent *vāc-yavācaka* relation. Only *āpta-vacana* (a trustworthy speaker's utterance) is authoritative; an untrustworthy speaker's word is not. The Veda is authoritative because it is composed by a *puruṣa* superior to ourselves — God; the *anityatva* of the Veda is proved by inference (the composition of sentences requires intelligent action). The Mīmāṃsaka *svataḥ-prāmāṇya-vāda* (validity self-given, only invalidity from external cause) is rebutted at length: prāmāṇya is *parataḥ* (from the *guṇa* of the cause, the absence of *doṣa*); otherwise erroneous cognitions would be impossible. The footnote tabulates the *Sarvadarśanasaṃgraha*'s four positions (Sāṃkhya: both *svataḥ*; Nyāya: both *parataḥ*; Bauddha: *aprāmāṇya svataḥ*, *prāmāṇya parataḥ*; Mīmāṃsā: *prāmāṇya svataḥ*, *aprāmāṇya parataḥ*).

en_simple_draft.text: *Ceṣṭā* (gesture — e.g. fingers drawn in mean 'come', fingers thrust out mean 'go away') is held by some Tāntrikas to be a distinct *pramāṇa*. Śrīdhara denies it: only one who already knows the conventional meaning of the gesture cognises an object through it; one ignorant of the convention does not. The relation is therefore not natural but *sāṅketika*, resting on *vyāpti-jñāna*; so gestural cognition is just *anumāna*.

en_simple_draft.text: *Upamāna* (analogy) is shown not to be an independent *pramāṇa*. 'Āpta' is the trustworthy person whose direct cognition reaches even supersensible objects such as *dharma* — the teacher. Example: a city-dweller who does not know the *gavaya* asks a forester (an *āpta*) what it is; the forester replies 'a *gavaya* is similar to a cow'; the resulting cognition of similarity is *upamiti*. en_simple_draft.text: *Dharma* is a property of man's *ātman* — not a potency inhering in the act performed. It causes happiness, the means of happiness, and final *mokṣa*. Śrīdhara refutes at length the Mīmāṃsaka *apūrva* doctrine: action (e.g. sacrifice) is momentary, yet its remote fruit (e.g. heaven) requires a persistent potency. The Mīmāṃsaka posits *apūrva* inhering either in the action or in the result; Śrīdhara replies that a śakti needs a substrate, the destroyed action cannot host it, and neither the future result nor any eternal substance such as *ākāśa* will do — so what persists must inhere in the *ātman*: it is *dharma* itself. The sacrifice is called 'dharma' only figuratively, as 'heaven' is applied figuratively to sandal-paste that yields happiness. *Dharma* is *sūkṣma* (super-sensuous) and perceptible only to yogis. The author then catalogues its means: the common virtues (*śraddhā*, *ahiṃsā*, *bhūta-hita*, *satya*, *asteya*, *brahmacarya*, *anabhidhyā*, *śauca*, *devatā-bhakti*, *upavāsa*, *apramāda*), the caste-specific duties of *brāhmaṇa, kṣatriya, vaiśya, śūdra*, the duties of the four *āśrama*s (*brahmacārin, gṛhastha, vānaprastha, sannyāsin*), the five *mahāyajña*s, *agnihotra*, and *yoga*-practice culminating in self-knowledge. Though *dharma* itself drives the cycle of birth and rebirth, *yoga-ja-dharma* matures into *tattva-jñāna* which yields the direct cognition of the *ātman*; *dharma* and *adharma* then cease, and *mokṣa* follows.

en_simple_draft.text: *Adharma*, like *dharma*, is a quality of the *ātman*. It is conducive to sin (a source of future *duḥkha*) and to actual *duḥkha*; it is imperceptible and destructible by experiencing its last item of pain. Its causes are (1) doing what scripture prohibits (*hiṃsā*, untruth, taking what is not given); (2) deliberate non-performance of enjoined obligatory acts; (3) *apramāda* — unconscious lapse of duty. Wilful evil with motive is *saṅkalpa-duṣṭi* ('impurity of intentions'); unwilled lapse falls under *apramāda*.

en_simple_draft.text: Śrīdhara's long *mokṣa* exposition — the bulkiest single block in this stretch. One who performs *dharma* with knowledge and without desire for fruits is reborn in a pure family; afflicted by *duḥkha*, he seeks an *ācārya*, receives the *ṣaṭ-padārtha-tattva-jñāna*, and matures it through *śravaṇa, manana, nididhyāsana*. *Tattva-jñāna* dissolves *avidyā* with its *vāsanā*s and *kāmanā*s; *vairāgya* arises; *rāga–dveṣa* cease, and fresh *dharma–adharma* stop being produced. Previously stored *dharma–adharma* burns down through experience; the residual *dharma* is of the *nivṛtti* kind — it yields the happiness of *santoṣa* and aversion to the body, then the happiness born of *ātma-sākṣātkāra*, then is itself extinguished. With the seed gone, when the present body falls no new body is taken: this *videhāvasthā* is *mokṣa*, like the extinguishing of fire whose fuel has burnt out. Śrīdhara defends the *jñāna-karma-samuccaya-vāda*: liberation is not from pure *jñāna* alone but from *jñāna* joined with the *nitya-naimittika* duties. Omitting *nitya-karma* generates sin (because *jīvana* is itself activity; at the appointed time *sandhyā* etc. *are* the prescribed activity; merely 'living' instead is a forbidden alternative). Hence even the *jīvanmukta*, until the body drops, must continue prescribed action. The Vedāntic view that the *ātman*'s nature is *ānanda* is refuted at length: after the loss of body and *indriya*s there is no cause for the experience of bliss; if *ānanda* belonged to *caitanya* by nature, it would have to be experienced in *saṃsāra* too. So *mokṣa* is just the cessation of the *ātma-viśeṣa-guṇa*s; the *ātman* abides in its own form alone.

ml_draft.text: *ശബ്ദ*ം *ആകാശ*ത്തിന്റെ ഗുണം — ശ്രവണ-ഗ്രാഹ്യം. ശ്രീധരൻ ശങ്കിക്കുന്നു: ആകാശത്തിന് സംഖ്യാദി മറ്റു ഗുണങ്ങളും ഉണ്ടല്ലോ — അതുകൊണ്ടു 'ആകാശ-ഗുണം' എന്നതു ലക്ഷണമാകുകയില്ല. സമാധാനം: *ശ്രവണേന്ദ്രിയ-ഗ്രാഹ്യം* എന്ന വിശേഷണംകൊണ്ടു ലക്ഷണം പര്യാപ്തം. ശബ്ദം *ക്ഷണികം* — ഉത്പന്നമായ ഉടനെത്തന്നെ നശിക്കും; നിത്യത്വ-വാദം (മീമാംസകം) അനുപപന്നം. പുനഃ-പ്രത്യഭിജ്ഞാനം — 'ഇതേ ശബ്ദംതന്നെ' — *സാദൃശ്യ-മൂലകം*, ദീപ-ജ്വാല ഒന്നായി തോന്നുന്നതുപോലെ. ശബ്ദം മൂന്നുവിധത്തിൽ *വിനാശിതം* — സ്വ-കാര്യത്താൽ (പ്രഥമം), സ്വ-കാരണത്താൽ (അന്ത്യം), ഉഭയത്താൽ (മധ്യമം). ഉത്പത്തി — സംയോഗ-വിഭാഗ-ശബ്ദത്താൽ. *വർണാത്മകം* (അ-ആദി അക്ഷരങ്ങൾ) — ആത്മ-മനഃ-സംയോഗം ⇒ വക്തൃ-ഇച്ഛ ⇒ പ്രയത്നം ⇒ ആത്മാ-വായു-സംയോഗം ⇒ വായു-ക്രിയ ⇒ കണ്ഠാദി-സ്ഥാന-സംഹതി ⇒ ആകാശ-സ്ഥാന-സംയോഗം ⇒ വർണ-ശബ്ദ-ഉത്പത്തി. *ധ്വന്യാത്മകം* (ശംഖ-ഭേരി ധ്വനി) — ദ്രവ്യ-ആകാശ-സംയോഗത്താൽ. *വീചീ-തരംഗ-ന്യായം* — ജല-വീചീപോലെ ശബ്ദ-തരംഗ-പരമ്പര; ഒരു ശബ്ദം മറ്റൊരു ശബ്ദത്തെ ജനിപ്പിച്ച് ശ്രോത്രേന്ദ്രിയത്തിലെത്തുമ്പോൾ ശ്രവണം. *ശ്രോത്രേന്ദ്രിയ-ശബ്ദ-സന്നികർഷ* — രണ്ടും അചലങ്ങളെങ്കിലും വീചീ-പരമ്പരയിലൂടെ വ്യാപാരം — ഇതാണ് ശ്രീധരന്റെ പ്രതിപാദ്യം. ഇതോടെ *ഗുണ-പദാർത്ഥ-ചര്‍ച്ച* സമാപിക്കുന്നു — കഥാ-ശ്ലോകത്തിൽ: 'ഈ ഗുണ-ഗ്രന്ഥം — യുക്തിയിൽനിന്നു ജനിച്ച് — രത്നഹാരംപോലെ ഹൃദയത്തിൽ ധരിക്കപ്പെടട്ടെ'; *'ഇതി ഗുണ-പദാർത്ഥഃ'*.

en_simple_draft.text: *Śabda* is the *guṇa* of *ākāśa*, perceptible by the ear. Objection: *ākāśa* has other guṇas (number etc.) — 'guṇa of ākāśa' alone is no proper definition. Reply: the definition is *śravaṇendriya-grāhya guṇa of ākāśa*. *Śabda* is *kṣaṇika* — destroyed at the moment after its production; the Mīmāṃsaka *nityatva* doctrine is rejected; recognition 'this is the same sound' rests on similarity, like the apparent identity of a continuous flame which is in fact a series. Śabda is counteracted three ways — by its effect (the first sound), by its cause (the last), by both (middle sounds). It is produced by *saṃyoga*, *vibhāga*, and *śabda* itself. *Varṇātmaka śabda* (the letters *a* etc.) arises in this sequence: *ātma-manas-saṃyoga* → desire to utter → *prayatna* → *ātma-vāyu-saṃyoga* → motion in the vāyu of the stomach → contact with throat/palate etc. → contact of *ākāśa* with those points → letter-sound. *Dhvanyātmaka śabda* (noise of a drum or conch) arises from contact between the substance and *ākāśa*. The *vīcī-taraṅga-nyāya* — like water-ripples, śabda generates a continuous series of śabda-waves; the last unit of the series in contact with the ear is what is heard. Since the ear does not move to the source and the source does not move to the ear, only the wave-series accounts for the perception. The chapter closes with the customary verse — may this *guṇa*-treatise, born of reasoning, be worn upon the heart like a necklace of pearls — and the colophon *iti guṇa-padārthaḥ*.
